p: Right, so those are ways to engage, um, that population, um, and make sure that they're aware of the options.
I'm just saying we should work with NYCHA. That's what I'm saying. I'm just— so that's what I'm saying, as another entity.
Yes, absolutely.

Okay, also there's a group called Options. I don't know if you work with Options. Options is out of Goddard Riverside, and basically it's, it's a very expensive fabulous— you can go there and say, I am interested in engineering and I need a full scholarship and they will tell you immediately, plus they give you lots of support. So I just— it's another tool. Um, I think there may be one other nonprofit that has options, but the young people that I work with, I send them— I say, hello, go to Options, because it gives you that kind of support. That it's a major, uh, database, very expensive for them to provide. So I just offer it as another place to go. Anybody's open to the whole city, and it's all free. Um, my final question is, what, uh, you finish college, uh, then what? Is there support after that, getting through either 2 years, 4 years, or whatever? How— is that something that it's also part of what you're doing when you're looking for a job?

So, we continue to support the young person when they finish college. They can, they can receive the stipend, the $60-a-day stipend for another 6 months, and in that time, we are continuing to provide support to them um, and then they have their Fair Future Coach. And depending on the housing that they moved into, we're working very closely with a program called Anthos Home, and they're doing some housing navigation services, and they provide a year of aftercare. So they provide some additional support, um, to help preserve the households so that, you know, if there's issues come up, they'll help the young person navigate so that they can maintain their housing. So we have a few, um, levers that we use to make sure that young people are supported, but the most important is the Fair Futures coach.
I know, I know. Congratulations, everybody.
Thank you, Council Member Brewer. Uh, quick question for students who may be parents: is there support for young people in this, in this system with child care?

Yes, I'm thinking about a case, um, particularly. So yes, we continue to work with, um, young people that are students. So depending on the university they attend, they may have some natural supports. Um, sometimes the young people will remain in their foster care placement, so we support the foster parent, for example, making sure that there's day care and there's, you know, there's babysitting when needed while the young person goes to school. That's where that stipend really becomes helpful because it allows the young person to have a little bit more financial freedom to provide support. So we definitely try to work with this young person and their child and make sure they're connected. And so that may mean in some cases they stay local, but there are universities that might also provide, um, supports for parenting students.
What is the most common major you've seen among young people in care?
Nursing is a big one. Social work, psychology is another big one. And I think computers are on the rise. That's what we're seeing.

Alright, we learned in the Preliminary Budget Hearing that FY26 funding for

FYSCI was $3.6 million and that the program is funded entirely by New York State. How has New York State funding increased over recent years as enrollments of students with a background in foster care has increased?

It's in— it's increased. Um, so the FYCSI budget, as you know, because it's a New York State funded program and it's at SUNY, CUNY, and the private colleges, we share the budget. So the overall budget may be more, but CUNY's allocation was $3.6 million. And so over the years we've had increases, um but our enrollment numbers have increased significantly as well. So it's, it's hard sometimes to keep pace with the budget and the enrollment, but we, we try to make it work.

So the next question as a follow-up: does CUNY believe current funding on the New York state is sufficient to meet the needs? What unmet needs currently exist? If you were to have more money, what else can you do?

We could always use more money, right? Um, yeah, I mean, I think there's ways to strengthen what we do right, we can, you know, our stipend that we give has stayed consistent over time.

That absolutely can increase. And I think the ways in which we support students with housing off campus would be one way that we can also look to, to secure, um, I mean, to use with additional secured funding. Um, right now we, the cost of, um, we, we cover on-campus housing only. Um, we don't cover students who are living in, in off-campus housing or in their own apartments.
Hmm, interesting.
However, if they're in the College Choice program, we can provide, um—
Off-campus.
Uh, uh, we can cover the cost for the off-campus housing.
Okay, um, okay, okay. Does CUNY plan to look for additional funding source for FY— CSI?

We're always, we're always looking for, um, additional supports. And I, and I would also say, you know, funding is always great, of course, you know, but just also just additional resources to support young people is, is ways that we're looking to make sure that we can support our students.
Um, there's a program that caught my attention recently in the SUNY— in the SUNY system called SUNY Reconnect Foster. Is that— does that program exist in CUNY?
We have a CUNY Reconnect program. Um, I don't know that it's specifically— it's not specifically designed for foster youth, it's for students who've stopped out.

Um, yeah, we're familiar CUNY Reconnect, but this one is— the one is CUNY, is specifically for students in foster care. So maybe you guys should look at that model and see how can we, um, duplicate that model on the CUNY level.

Yeah, it's a great idea. Yeah, so the program is when they drop out of college to get them back in school. Um, what does CUNY do to reach out to students who have left CUNY before graduating to try to enroll them? That's what this CUNY Reconnect is for.
Right.

So it's the same model as the CUNY Reconnect. Well, how do we get young people back into the system? Mhm. Um, so that's, that's, that's it. Um, how does CUNY coordinate with ACS as

an agency as well as with providers that ACS contracts with to provide services? Do you feel the coordinations are adequate?

Absolutely. I have a great relationship. I, you know, Sonia and I are on speed dial with each other. Um, we're constantly coordinating and I'm always looking for resources. So, um, McKeema mentioned At the Table and City Living. Those are other, uh, city organizations that we also regularly— Anthos is another one. We're always looking for ways to connect our students because we know that we can't, we can't do everything. And so we look to make sure that students have what they need, and some of these programs can support them post-graduation the way we cannot. So we wanna make sure our students are connected to all of these programs. So we have a really good relationship with a lot of these external organizations as well.
Well, that's one of the things, um, I think Chair Stevens and I can agree on. Sometimes agencies don't talk to each other, but yet they're doing the same work.
Right.
So I think the work overlap, and there should be relationships there.
Absolutely.
Go ahead.

I wanted to add that, um, at ACS, we meet with providers on a monthly basis. So we meet with our ed specialists, um, college specialists, case planners at times join these monthly meetings, um, and we invite— spicy— we invite financial aid offices to provide workshops to— for our providers, um, and other subject matter experts to make sure that our providers are getting the information they need so they could turn key that information over to the students. Um, the meetings are usually very well attended, um, and CUNY is definitely, um, very well in the room.
Um, does CUNY plan to do outreach to more students with background in foster care either while they're in high school or after they come to CUNY? If so, how does that happen? Do you do the outreach?

We generally do that through ACS or ACS, you know, the foster care agencies. So

we'll go through those programs. So I'll connect with an agency and I'll come into their, you know, to the foster care agency and do presentations. Or I remember one time we did like a FAFSA workshop to try to help students complete their FAFSA in the room, like in the moment, and get help in that moment. So we do that through the foster care agencies.
You said you had coaches and social workers. What does their caseloads look like? What are the numbers?

So our social work interns have- the caseload can range from 30 to 40. Now that's, um, sounds like a very high number for, uh, internships, and it usually is. But remember, our students don't connect every week or every day. So our social work interns are in twice a week, and they have this caseload, this higher caseload, because students don't connect every single day. They might connect once a month, they might connect twice a month, they might, when there's an issue, connect every day. And then when there's a month that there's no issue, there's— they may not connect at all. So it depends on the number of interns. We've also— we are also able to increase the number of

interns. So if I'm looking at our enrollment and I'm looking at our interns, I'll say, oh, we have a lot more students this year, we need a lot more interns. So we've— we currently are hosting 10 social work interns. We've hosted up to 12, and we can keep— we can take in more interns if we start to see a trend where— because we do also see a trend where FYCSI students are connecting more to interns. So when interns leave in May, the interns— the next group comes in in September. And so sometimes we'll have students saying, where's my intern? Where's my intern? So students are connecting more. So we may drop the caseload and get more interns.
And how can the City Council help, um, in supporting students with a background in foster care who are enrolled in CUNY?
Do you want to take that first?
Um, money. Well, we know that, but what else?

So I think, you know, we're talking about apps, like, if you— real talk, like, how can we make apps and, and different pieces of materials that we can share? I think what I'm hearing a little bit— I'm not saying that every child

in care— I know they're not getting all the information, but there's a group of children that have been adopted, have kin gap, that have been reunified. They are eligible for the programs, but they're no longer physically attached to a foster care provider. So I just wrote myself a note. We have 3 agencies that provide post-adoption kin gap services. Remember, their case is closed, but sometimes those families still have bumps in the road, and those 3 agencies are working with those families. So I just wrote myself a note: we need to connect you to those—
Yes.
Programs, right? Children are reunified, they're back with mom and dad, they're back with grandma, they're back with whoever. They're not part of, uh-
Someone like me.

Right? So how do we get— how do we share that information with all of those parents? 1,700 children were reunified in Fiscal Year '25 for ACS. Not all of them are college age, but they're gonna go to high school, they might be

interested in college. So how do we make sure, 'cause those, some of those children will be eligible for these services that CUNY offers or SUNY offers, but how do we share that information? I don't know, I don't have the answer today, but I think that it's a good, so City Council, if you wanna brainstorm and we figure out how we can make sure that those parents are also aware, um, that their, their children may be eligible for, uh, um, particular types of services. So I think those are— and well, and let me take that a step further because yes, we— ours— our eligibility requirement for our students are students who were in care at the age of 13. So the wonderful thing about FYCSI is that, as McKeema said, your age currently doesn't matter. You can be 30, you can be 40, you can be 50 years old and still be eligible for FYCSI, which is a wonderful thing. And because they weren't in care, they have not been in care since 14, 15, or 16, they also don't have the same kinds of supports as a student, as a young person who's leaving care, going right into college. So one of the ways that we could use support funding and other— because I keep talking about

reason, because yes, money is, is great. Yes, give us all the money, right? But there's also the resources. And so I think about relationships, I think about resources, one of our, uh, the biggest needs for our students is housing. So where ACS can help students with housing, with, um, vouchers for Section 8, for NYCHA, and I don't wanna speak too much. I, I think that's, that's still the, the, what the, you know, there's priority housing for foster youth. There is no priority housing for former foster youth.

Right. There's no prior— there's no priority voucher for, for, for former foster youth. So if a student is 30 years old, 45 years old, and is living in our dorm because they don't have housing, when they graduate, they have to move. I don't have priority housing for them. So any, any advocacy, any support, any resources, any connections that, that we could, that we could have to, to support students that don't have those same supports because they haven't been in care in 10 years, in 20 years, in 5 years, is another way that we could use the support.

Yeah, I mean, I think also too, even thinking about— that's our whole fight around CityFHEPS of like people who need the support, they would get it. And so like this would be a holistic thing because instead of saying like, we're gonna prioritize and then putting folks who need services against each other, right? Because we have homeless runaway youth, right. We have all these different categories to give people housing. So I think we all should be collectively working together to support the CityFHEP, the CityFHEP voucher push that we've been having at the City Council level. And also pushing NYCHA to be able to get those vacancies up and going.
Absolutely.
And I know that we've been talking about that a lot too. And I know that like Gale was even pushing the conversation around
Absolutely.
Like, we have a housing crisis, and so we need to all be working together. So we hear you and we wanna work in partnership with you.
I would love it.

And continue to do advocacy around that because the need is real. And I think even pointing out the need for, um, folks who are aged out of foster care who needs housing, like, those are all the folks who are in the DSS shelters.
Absolutely.
And all those things that we're always yelling about.

Absolutely. The other thing I would say around policies, I mean, you're the City Council, so the other supportive is, you know, I was having a conversation with an organization who does— who, who has— or who has sometimes had— has vouchers. Living in a dorm is not considered at-risk in terms of housing, in terms of emergency vouchers. I would beg to differ. You know, students, if they graduate, it— you know, I— we all know that, you know, you can get a job after graduation, but sometimes you have to wait for your paycheck, you have to save up a little money, you need first month's rent, deposit. That funding is not there. If that's not considered at-risk housing, I'm not sure what is, because once you graduate, that you can't live in the dorm anymore.
We want to make sure that young people are also staying in stable homes. Sometimes when we give them the vouchers, the housings don't match-

Um, where the young people are. They're unsafe. We saw NYCHA housing that was not safe, and they had to move the young person with their child. Child was born in care as well. So, um, just one last question, Chair Stevens. Mental health, we must talk about that.
Absolutely.
Do you provide mental health support?

So we, we provide, um, we don't provide it directly. We provide casework counseling, we provide casework management. That's what our social work interns do. So one of the things where we call our social work internship program for our FYSE students is individualized intensive case management. We meet you where you're at. And so if all you need is, I need help finding a job, then that's what we do. But if what you need is, I need help finding mental health therapy, then that's what we do.

If you just need somebody to to because you're just having a really bad day and nobody— that's what we do. So we don't provide it directly. We're not a mental health organization. I am a social worker. I work with a team of social work supervisors. We're all licensed social workers. We supervise social work interns. So the mental health is there, and we bring it into the work in, in our way of being, um, in terms of mental health. But if a student needs mental health therapy treatment, then we will refer them out, and we often do. And we can start with our counseling centers at CUNY and then refer them out for long-term counseling and psychiatric services if they need it.
How long is the wait?

For counseling centers? It differs by campus. So we will use counseling centers, or we will go outside of CUNY, whatever's first. There's also some organizations that specifically do mental health treatment for foster youth. There's an organization that I just got connected to that I'm in the midst of connecting to that does, um, therapy through the arts, creative

arts, for former foster youth, for current and former youth. So I'm always out looking for friends. It's all what I was— I always— I can always use a friend. Um, and so I look and see.
Chair Stevens?

Sure. Oh, look, my earpiece is coming off. Alright. Um, I just have a couple more questions. Um, what percentage of foster youth in Fair Futures attend CUNY institutions? And what are the high, um, high school graduation and college enrollment and college persistence rates for youth participating in Fair Futures.

Currently, of the youth that are in College Choice, 301, which I think is 63%, um, attend CUNY of the 471, and the majority of those children— I think I have the data point, do we have the data point? Um, uh, received Fair Futures, sorry. So of the children that go to CUNY, 224— so 301 are in College Choice, 224— thank you, Stephanie— um, are connected to Fair Futures.

What specific supports do Fair Futures coaches provide to youth who are interested in enrolling in college, including

assistance with college application, financial aid, college, um, selection, and transition planning?

So the Fair Futures coaches will provide a lot of support. We work very closely with the Center for Fair Futures, and they do a lot of training and provide technical assistance on a variety of areas that are inter— that a young person in foster care, housing, education, workforce. And so through their platform, they have, um, access to tr— they, the coaches can use this virtual platform and they get information around college, the application project— process, um, college guides, so on and so forth. And so they're able to use that information while they're working with the young person. But in addition to the coach, as Sonia mentioned, the agencies have education specialists. They can support young people through that process. and also their case planner.
Are, um, are Fair Futures coaches or staff involved in supporting students once they're enrolled in CUNY, and if so, how is that support structured?

Yes, so Fair Futures coaches continue to work with young people, you know, whether

they're going to CUNY, SUNY, if they're not in— going to college, um, and they provide coaching, and they're really working on individual goals. It may have to do with their academic goals, their work goals, maybe there's a goal around mental health, a goal around housing, and through this Fair Futures model, they are, um, provided the support to help reach those particular goals.
What is the current funding structure for Fair Futures, including the balance between city funding and private philanthropy?

So Fair Futures started in 2019, and that was a public-private partnership. At that time, the city invested about $10 million, and over each of the last few years, the number has increased. In Fiscal Year '23, that money was baselined at $30 million, so the city funds the program completely. That's not to say that each agency may have their own grants and other, um, foundation support that supports their Fair Futures or their foster care programming. But the city, um, increased the funding and baselined it in 2023. And then in this past fiscal year, um, we increased the funding to about $34 million and we're on track for next year

to be around $42 million. And then the goal when we're fully scaled will be, ah, around $54 million.
Are there established protocols to share systems between— Fair Future providers and College Choice staff to track referrals, um, confirm enrollment, and monitor students' progress?
So that's a lot of what Sonia does, and so I'll, I'll turn it over to her to provide a response.

Yes, um, we are consistently, um, sharing data with each other to ensure that the students who— the youth who are, um, in Fair Futures and have coaches, um, are connected to the College Choice program. We meet monthly to talk through technical assistance to ensure that, um, resources are being connected back to our providers, um, and our students.

Can I just make a clarification regarding the Fair Futures funding? I get my calendar year and fiscal years a little messed up, right? Okay, so for Fiscal Year '23, I was correct, we did baseline the dollars at $30 million. At the start of Fiscal Year '25, which was actually the

summer of 2024, we were at $34 million, in Fiscal Year '26 is $43 million, and this July, Fiscal Year '27, we'll be on track to be at $54 million.

Okay. Both the Fair Futures and College Choice programs are difficult, uh, to identify within ACS budget since they do not have their own budget code. Will you work with our, um, finance staff to identify historical percentages and present, um, present spending on those programs? What are the, um, respective budgets for Fair Futures and College Choice in FY 2026?
So the respective budgets for Fiscal Year '26 is $43,664,269 for Fair Futures, and College Choice is $50,698,921. And yes-
Those are really specific numbers. Could you please email that?
Yes.
Thank you.
So, uh, you didn't write that down? No. Um, and yes, and yes, our finance team is willing to, you know, work with whoever to create budget codes.
Thank you.
It won't be me, but the finance team will do it.
It won't be me either. But no, um, thank you so much. Those are all questions I have.
I had a quick question. If a student wanna pursue a graduate degree, uh, what type of support is in place for them?

So, sorry, so FYCSI does not support beyond the bachelor's degree. So we connect students as much as possible to whatever grants are out there. Um, because we started under Opportunity Programs, um, Opportunity Programs do have a GOP program, a Graduate Opportunity Program. And so if we happen to have a foster youth that is eligible for a program such as that, we, you know, connect them to that, or just any, any grants or, or resources that are out there for them. But unfortunately, the funding, current funding for FYCSI is only until the bachelor's level.

I lied, I'm back. Um, as coordination between these programs has strengthened, what gaps remain in delivering historic supports for young people with foster care experience,

particularly during key transition points in college? And, um, I guess this is talking about Fair Futures and, um, college success programs and things like that.

In terms of gaps, I mean, I think we identified some, making sure everyone in care is aware of the program. Um, so we have to make sure that the workforce, the case planners, and the coaches know about the program and know how best to, um, reach out to others for help. I think we can also, you know, continue to strengthen our coordination, making sure that all of the foster care agencies are involved in, um, learning about the programs and the supports at CUNY, um, and then also College Choice. Sonia, do you have other gaps?
So one of the things we try to— like, so we have data agreements, and so we— I think what we— the next step —foster care data is very protected.
Mhm.

Um, we do have a data sharing agreement with, um, New York City Public Schools. I don't believe we have a formal data sharing with CUNY, and so we probably could follow up with our

business law team to see if that is something that we can, um, maybe do a little bit more matching or even maybe on an aggregate level. So we have to— we don't wanna, you know, again, the foster care data is very protected and we wanna preserve that, but that might be something that we can look to see because that might allow us to— for example, if there was a kid in foster care, 24-hour placement, but in, um, the CUNY program that not part of College Choice, there are some other benefits we could provide that, that young person. So data sharing might help catch some of those gaps, but, um, that would be something we'd have to explore.

Well, one of the things that I'm seeing here that some providers, um, the questions even around, like, that obviously the supports are meaningful, but the access to sometimes has delays and sometimes it is really time-consuming. Um, how could, how can we, how clearly do young people understand the distinctions and purpose of each program? So like even the, the amount sometimes, and what changes would you recommend to ensure that support reaches students more quickly at a moment when it is most needed?

One of the things, um, College Choice, um, is able to support as many young people because we really want to make sure that all of the financial aid, all of the scholarships are applied before we then, um, if we have to contribute. So that does create sometimes— because the bursar's office is like, you know, right, but they're still waiting to hear from the Pell Grant and from this grant and this grant. And sometimes even family court will get involved, like ACS needs to but we really have to kind of do this dance. And I know that creates anxiety for kids in, in, in school, right? Because you may be getting messages and emails. So that is something that we try to communicate and provide support during that nuance. And then of course, making sure that we're still able to— and New York Foundling is, is our great partner in this work— is as, you know, if there are challenges that come up, whether it's school, whether, um, it's an emotional or a social nature, making sure that we are providing those wraparound services as quickly as possible.

Sometimes because they're living in the dorm, it's different than when you're in a foster care placement that someone might be, you know, have eyes on you every day. So we have to just, you know, make sure that we are able to support young people and they know where to turn if they have a crisis.

I mean, even with that, um, and again, like, they're saying, the provider is saying that authorization and verification um, and handoffs can, can determine impact. But from your perspective, what are some common protocols and Administration bottlenecks that slow down this process and supports? And I think you said some of it is like sometimes family court getting involved and like it's, you know, it's all these different things. Um, where, um, where are some places you think that can be streamlined to kind of help support that work, especially in these moments of crisis? Because it sounds like sometimes, although with all these supports and how it has all these good intentions, there's still a lot of bottleneck. And like, we know that navigating college in general is crazy because I just remember just always being like,

oh, okay, I have another email. Oh, I'm getting kicked out. Like, it— like, and that's— it's a lot.
Imagine going to school when there was an email. But yes, I understand.
Oh, we had email. I'm not that old. Dang. So what did they do, send a letter? Like how did that work?
Oh, so sad. I don't even remember, but we didn't have emails or that much.

How did they get that information? A letter sounds crazy. I know, it's so crazy. A letter is like— it's 7 days later now. I'm like, what's happening? I'm sorry, young people, they're looking at us like, what do you mean?

I know, sometimes I wish the documentation wasn't needed. You're in care, you're in school, you're accepted. I think that the documentation piece for our young, our young, uh, folks, it's— it is grueling at times because they do have to navigate going into their Bursar office and going to get their enrollment verification, and timelines sometimes don't match up. But I think, um,

because we at ACS are overseeing the application process and through that RFP process— that's a new implementation this year— we're able to really work quicker with our providers and directly with the students when issues come up. We don't have contracts with the university offices to get that information on the back end, which is kind of like on my wish list.
Um, and so everybody can hear.
The wish list of the back end partnership. Just send it to us.
Alright, great. Um, putting it out in the universe.
But what we have done is develop partnerships with those respective offices at various, um, universities.

So if it made more sense for us to just do it on the back channel, why hasn't that been something that's been pursued? It's, um, it's the same thing, you know, mentioned in terms of the confidentiality. It's that when our youth are in school, they are considered independent adults, and the communication, you know, has to come from the

student. Um, there are FERPAs and HIPAAs that sometimes can help with that, but even dependent on the university, if that is in place, they still may say back off, we need to speak to the student, the student needs to lead this charge.

I mean, I get that students should lead the charge and we want them to be responsible, but like, some of it sounds like it's administrative stuff that like we should really just be talking about being like, here's the paperwork. They've been in care. This makes more sense. So, um, hopefully we can like figure that out. Cause that, that sounds—

And then just to piggyback on what Sonia said, the documentation is essential because we use that information for our claiming purposes. Like we have to verify that they're in care and that allows us to then draw down JP funds and what other state dollars so that we can really continue to expand the program. So, we can look at how best to streamline. Um, we've done that a little bit in some of the other, um, pieces of our work not related to College Choice, but just in general to make life a little easier for

foster care providers so they don't have to send so many documents to us. So we can look at the process and see what we— where we might be able to give some easement.
Yeah, well, those are all the questions I have for now. Thank you.

Does, um, College Choice have slots or it's, it's on a rolling basis. So this year our budget afforded 430, um, young people. So I mean, beginning of Fiscal Year '26 was July 1st of 2025. But as I mentioned, because not every student takes the same amount of money, we were able to serve 471 youth and stay within our budget. So, um, some of those documents and those different things allow us to have a little bit more flexibility because in our able to apply for more scholarships, more financial aid. So your balance may be zero, your balance may be, you know, $1,000, and we're able to just serve— well, maybe yours is zero too, but that just allows us so that when we have, um, you know, students in universities where there is a balance, we can support them too. It's really important. College Choice allows young people to have a choice. And just like, um, you know, young

people, some people want to go to this particular school, some people want to be someplace warm, some people are interested in anthropology. And so College Choice does let young people kind of go where they feel like they'll excel, um, the most. And so we want to keep that flexibility as much as possible.
So there is never a waitlist for students to get into the program?

So no, for— and for FYCSI, we accept students on a rolling basis. So the app— we get most of our students at the beginning of the year, obviously, but then every month OCFS is verifying eligible students because students can continue to apply throughout the year. So, all the way up to, like, March, April, we're getting lists from students that are applying to the program and we bring them right in. Once they are found eligible by OCFS, they're in.
Okay, thank you. Thank you. Yeah, we're done for real. Thank you.
